Following several mishaps in which Tamas got lost in a Macy's store and pulled a fire alarm in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Breuer decided to build a house in the town of New Canaan, Connecticut, in the city's northeastern suburbs. Land was cheaper in New Canaan than in the city itself

facts.fact: The house is an early example of Breuer's 'long house' or 'long box' designs and was influenced by Bauhaus principles.
facts.quote: The design of the house was influenced by the Bauhaus principles that had guided Marcel Breuer's early career. It is an early example of Breuer's "long house" or "long box" designs, a style he later refined with the construction of the Breuer House III in Cape Cod, Massachusetts.

facts.fact: Breuer experimented with balloon framing, cantilevering the upper storey out from a set of cables.
facts.quote: In designing the Breuer House II, Breuer experimented extensively with balloon framing, cantilevering the upper story outward from a set of cables.

facts.fact: It is a wooden structure with steel suspension cables supporting the cantilevered upper storey, which projects on all sides over a lower storey embedded in the hill.
facts.quote: The Breuer House II is a wooden structure with steel suspension cables supporting the cantilevered upper story.

facts.fact: The cantilevers sagged: temporary supports had to be reinstalled soon after completion, and later shoring walls and columns reduced the cantilevers' effect.
facts.quote: Over the years, the cantilevered section has been shored up with additional walls to deal with sagging, blunting the cantilevers' effect.

facts.fact: The main living areas are on the upper level, with bedrooms to the south and family rooms to the north, laid out to capture winter sunlight from the south.
facts.quote: The main living areas are placed on the upper level, with the bedrooms to the south, the family rooms to the north, and a kitchen and dining area in between. The layout was intended to capture as much sunlight as possible during the winter (when the sun was low and to the south), while also taking advantage of morning light.

facts.fact: The house became part of the 'Harvard Five' circle of modernist architects in New Canaan.
facts.quote: Breuer became part of the Harvard Five group of architects who lived in the town, along with Noyes, Johnson, John M. Johansen, and Landis Gores.

facts.fact: Architectural Record wrote that Breuer had done a house which would undoubtedly find its way into future texts on architecture.
facts.quote: When the house was completed, the Architectural Record wrote that "Breuer has done a house which undoubtedly will find its way into future texts on architecture".

facts.fact: The Dongda (East) Hall was built in 857 AD during the Tang dynasty and is the third earliest preserved timber structure in China.
facts.quote: The major hall of the temple is the Dongda Hall, built in 857 AD, during the Tang dynasty (618–907). It is the third earliest preserved timber structure in China.

facts.fact: It is the only building to combine Tang-dynasty architecture, sculpture, mural painting and calligraphic inscriptions in one structure, known as the 'Four Supremacies'.
facts.quote: The Dongda Hall is the only building to contain Tang-dynasty architecture, sculpture, mural painting, and calligraphic inscriptions in a single structure, known as the "Four Supremacies", and the temple is regarded as China's foremost national treasure of ancient architecture.

facts.fact: Architectural historians Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin rediscovered the temple in 1937.
facts.quote: The temple was rediscovered by architectural historians Liang Sicheng and Lin Huiyin in 1937, while an older smaller hall at Nanchan Temple was discovered by the same team a year later.

facts.fact: The temple was rebuilt in 857 with the Dongda Hall; a woman named Ning Gongyu provided most of the funds and a monk named Yuancheng led construction.
facts.quote: Twelve years later in 857 the temple was rebuilt, with the Dongda Hall being built on the former site of a three-storey pavilion. A woman named Ning Gongyu provided most of the funds needed to construct the hall, and its construction was led by a monk named Yuancheng.

facts.fact: Its hillside site encloses it on three sides and opens west to a valley, so the temple faces west, unlike most Chinese temples, which face south.
facts.quote: This topography dictated the temple's unusual east–west orientation, unlike most Chinese temples, which face south, Foguang Temple faces west, with its principal hall built against the eastern hillside at the highest point of the complex.

facts.fact: The buildings are arranged on three terraced platforms ascending the slope from west to east.
facts.quote: The temple's buildings are arranged on three terraced platforms ascending the slope from west to east.

facts.fact: The highest terrace is raised on a massive stone retaining wall reached by a stairway, and supports the Tang-dynasty East Great Hall with a panoramic westward view.
facts.quote: The lowest and broadest terrace contains the Jin dynasty Wenshu Hall; the middle terrace holds subsidiary courtyards; and the highest terrace, raised approximately 13 metres above the courtyard on a massive stone retaining wall reached by a stairway, supports the Tang-dynasty East Great Hall, which commands a panoramic westward view across the valley.

facts.fact: The hall is a single-storey structure seven bays by four, supported by inner and outer sets of columns.
facts.quote: It is a single storey structure measuring seven bays by four or 34 by 17.7 metres (110 by 58 ft), and is supported by inner and outer sets of columns.

facts.fact: Each column carries a complicated bracket set containing seven bracket types, one-half as high as the column itself.
facts.quote: On top of each column is a complicated set of brackets containing seven different bracket types that are one-second as high as the column itself.

facts.fact: A lattice ceiling conceals much of the roof frame from view.
facts.quote: The hall has a lattice ceiling that conceals much of the roof frame from view.

facts.fact: The auditorium at Arizona State University in Tempe is considered one of Frank Lloyd Wright's last public commissions and was built from 1962 to 1964.
facts.quote: The auditorium, which bears the name of former ASU President Grady Gammage, is considered to be one of the last public commissions of American architect Frank Lloyd Wright. It was built from 1962 to 1964.

facts.fact: President Grady Gammage wanted a unique facility for the campus after a 1956 roof collapse left the combination auditorium/gymnasium unusable.
facts.quote: The process that led to construction of the auditorium began in 1957 when incumbent university President Grady Gammage desired a unique facility for the ASU campus. In 1956, a collapsed roof rendered the school's combination auditorium/gymnasium unusable.

facts.fact: Gammage recruited his friend Frank Lloyd Wright, who based the design, with budget-related alterations, on a circular opera house he had conceived for Baghdad.
facts.quote: Gammage recruited his friend Frank Lloyd Wright to design the new building. He would, with various budget related alterations, base its design on a circular opera house that he had conceptualized for the city of Baghdad sometime prior upon the invitation of Iraqi King Faisal II.

facts.fact: Wright and Gammage both died in 1959, and Wright's protégé William Wesley Peters completed the building.
facts.quote: Wright and Gammage both died in 1959, leaving Wright's protégé William Wesley Peters to undertake completion of the auditorium.

facts.fact: Fifty concrete columns support the round roof, which has a pattern of interlocking circles.
facts.quote: Fifty concrete columns support the round roof with its pattern of interlocking circles.

facts.fact: Twin 'flying buttress' pedestrian ramps extend from the north and east sides to connect the building to the parking lot.
facts.quote: Twin "flying buttress" pedestrian ramps extending 200 feet (61 m) from the north and east sides of the structure connect the building to the parking lot.

facts.fact: The stage can be adapted for opera, theatricals, musicals, concerts and lectures.
facts.quote: The stage can be adapted for opera, theatricals, musicals, concerts, and lectures.

facts.fact: It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985.
facts.quote: ASU Gammage was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985.

facts.fact: John Andrews designed the Cameron Offices in a brutalist structuralism style for the National Capital Development Commission; they were built between 1970 and 1976.
facts.quote: The Cameron Offices are a group of former government offices commissioned by the National Capital Development Commission and designed by John Andrews in the brutalist structuralism style of architecture. The offices were constructed between 1970 and 1976

facts.fact: They were the first major buildings in Belconnen and formed part of the original town plan for a compact, pedestrian-oriented scheme.
facts.quote: The Cameron Offices were the first major buildings to be built in Belconnen. They formed part of the original town plan, in which the aim was to provide a relatively compact pedestrian-oriented scheme on a north–south axis following the slope of the land from housing to the south through the office areas, transport interchange and shopping centre on to the man-made Lake Ginninderra, which was to have cultural buildings and housing along its shore.

facts.fact: Andrews returned to Australia from Toronto to take the job, wanting a truly Australian modern large-scale building suited to Australian conditions.
facts.quote: Andrews was chosen by Sir John Overall of the National Capital Development Commission as the architect, mainly on the recommendation of Professor Gordon Stephenson. Andrews, who was a professor of architecture at the University of Toronto at the time, returned to Australia specifically to undertake the project. Andrews wished to create a truly Australian modern large-scale building suited to Australian conditions

facts.fact: The complex used in-situ concrete for much of the Mall and precast, mostly post-tensioned concrete for the office wings, with precasting done on site.
facts.quote: Built over a 2.4-hectare (6-acre) site, the complex was constructed with in-situ concrete – much of the Mall, and precast concrete (mostly post-tensioned) – the office wings, with precasting being done on site.

facts.fact: It won worldwide acclaim through a listing on the Union of International Architects Heritage register.
facts.quote: The design qualities of the Cameron Offices were recognised as significant at the time of their construction and won worldwide acclaim through a listing on the Union of International Architects Heritage register.

facts.fact: Voids within the wings created wind-tunnel effects and the sprawl made walking between offices slow, making the buildings unpopular with many public servants.
facts.quote: The nature of the voids within the wings resulted in windtunnel effects, which combined with the buildings' concrete design to make them unpleasant to walk around, particularly in the winter.

facts.fact: Only three of the original nine wings and the pedestrian bridge remain; two of the wings were converted to student accommodation.
facts.quote: Today, only three of the original nine wings (3, 4 and 5) and the pedestrian bridge remain. Wing 3 was previously occupied by Commonwealth Superannuation Corporation (CSC), the organisation responsible for providing superannuation products and services to government employees. Wings 4 and 5 have since been converted from government offices into student accommodation for the nearby University of Canberra.

facts.fact: Robarts Library is the main humanities and social sciences library of the University of Toronto Libraries, on the St. George campus.
facts.quote: The John P. Robarts Research Library, commonly referred to as Robarts Library (ROH-barts), is the main humanities and social sciences library of the University of Toronto Libraries and the largest individual library at the university, located on the St. George campus in downtown Toronto.

facts.fact: It is an example of brutalist architecture: a towering structure on an equilateral triangular footprint with triangular geometric patterns throughout.
facts.quote: The library building is an example of brutalist architecture. Its towering main structure rests on an equilateral triangular footprint and features extensive use of triangular geometric patterns throughout.

facts.fact: It is the main part of a three-tower complex with the Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library and the Claude T. Bissell Building.
facts.quote: It forms the main component of a three-tower complex that also includes the Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library and the Claude T. Bissell Building, which houses the Faculty of Information.

facts.fact: Mathers & Haldenby Architects headed the design, consulting with the New York firm Warner, Burns, Toan & Lunde, which specialised in precast concrete buildings.
facts.quote: The design of the Robarts Library complex was headed by Mathers & Haldenby Architects with consultation from Warner, Burns, Toan & Lunde, the New York architectural firm whose earlier works included the libraries at Cornell and Brown universities and who specialized in precast concrete buildings.

facts.fact: Construction ran from 1968 to 1973, and the initial plan was expanded by three storeys during the Canadian Centennial celebrations.
facts.quote: Coinciding with the Canadian Centennial celebrations, the initial plan was expanded to add three more storeys to the original design. Construction of the library began in 1968 and completed in 1973

facts.fact: Each side of the triangle is 330 feet, the length of a Canadian football field, and from the southeast corner the building appears as a peacock.
facts.quote: The building rests on an equilateral triangle footprint with each side measuring 330 feet (100 m), the same length as a Canadian football field from goal post to goal post. The building is oriented such that one side of the equilateral triangle faces west while the other two sides face northeast and southeast. From the southeast corner, the building appears as a peacock.

facts.fact: The concrete elevation varies in texture: smooth horizontal lines and rough vertical ones, with steel-framed bay windows reminiscent of medieval overhanging towers.
facts.quote: The elevation is mostly concrete, albeit differing in textures and directionality: smooth concrete lines the façade in a horizontal manner, the rough concrete lining vertically. The steel-framed windows are situated onto the bays protruding from the façade, and are reminiscent of overhanging towers in medieval castle architecture.

facts.fact: Fourteen storeys plus two underground floors, with raised podia and a suspended fourth floor; a mezzanine connects it to the neighbouring towers.
facts.quote: Comprising fourteen storeys, plus two underground floors, the brutalist and futurist structure features raised podia and a suspended fourth floor. A mezzanine level physically connects Robarts Library to the Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library building at its southeastern side, and to the Claude T. Bissell Building, housing the Faculty of Information, at its northeastern side.

facts.fact: Alvar Aalto designed the library, the main municipal public library of Rovaniemi, Finland.
facts.quote: Rovaniemi Library is the main municipal public library of the city of Rovaniemi, Finland.

facts.fact: It was part of rebuilding the city after the Lapland War, in which up to 90% of Rovaniemi's building stock was destroyed.
facts.quote: The building where the library used to operate was, along with up to 90% of Rovaniemi's building stock, destroyed during the Lapland War by the retreating German forces, necessitating the rebuilding of the city centre.

facts.fact: Aalto's town plan, the 'Reindeer Antler Plan', has five arterial roads forming the shape of a reindeer antler.
facts.quote: Aalto's eventual design, approved in 1946, is called Poronsarvikaava (literally, "Reindeer Antler Plan"), and incorporates five arterial roads forming the shape of a reindeer antler.

facts.fact: The library sits at the centre of the plan in the 'Aalto Centre', with the Lappia Hall and city hall, and the complex is protected as a nationally important built cultural environment.
facts.quote: At the centre of the plan, a complex of Aalto-designed public and administrative buildings, commonly referred to as 'Aalto Centre', comprises the Lappia Hall arts and conference venue and the Rovaniemi city hall alongside the library. The complex has been designated and protected by the Finnish Heritage Agency as a nationally important built cultural environment

facts.fact: The library building was completed in 1965.
facts.quote: The library building was completed in 1965.

facts.fact: The layout is a long rectangular office wing and a central fan-shaped area for lending and reading.
facts.quote: The overall layout of the building consists of a long, rectangular office wing, and a central, fan-shaped area housing the main lending section and reading areas.

facts.fact: The reading areas sit in a lower-level, recessed 'reading well', a signature feature of many of Aalto's libraries.
facts.quote: The reading areas are situated in a lower-level, recessed 'reading well', a signature feature of many of Aalto's library designs.

facts.fact: The fan-shaped section has extensive roof lights to bring maximum natural daylight onto the shelves along the interior walls.
facts.quote: The fan-shaped section has extensive roof lights designed to allow the maximum amount of natural daylight to enter the building, especially falling on the bookshelves positioned along the interior walls.

facts.fact: The exterior roof is clad with copper plates.
facts.quote: The exterior roof is clad with copper plates.

facts.fact: Teatro Colón is a historic opera house in Buenos Aires that National Geographic considers one of the ten best opera houses in the world.
facts.quote: The Teatro Colón (English: Colón Theatre) is a historic opera house in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

facts.fact: A survey by acoustics expert Leo Beranek found it has the best acoustics for opera and the second best for concerts in the world.
facts.quote: According to a survey carried out by the acoustics expert Leo Beranek among leading international opera and orchestra directors, the Teatro Colón has the room with the best acoustics for opera and the second best for concerts in the world.

facts.fact: The present theatre replaced an original theatre that opened in 1857 and opened in 1908 with Verdi's Aida after a 20-year process.
facts.quote: The present Colón replaced an original theatre which opened in 1857. Towards the end of the century, it became clear that a new theatre was needed, and after a 20-year process, the present theatre opened on 25 May 1908, with Giuseppe Verdi's Aïda.

facts.fact: The cornerstone was laid in 1889 under architect Francesco Tamburini and his pupil Vittorio Meano, who designed a theatre in the Italian style.
facts.quote: The cornerstone of the present Teatro Colón was laid in 1889 under the direction of architect Francesco Tamburini and his pupil, Vittorio Meano, who designed a theatre in the Italian style on a scale and with amenities which matched those in Europe.

facts.fact: Delays followed from financial difficulties, arguments about location, and the deaths of Tamburini (1891), Meano (1904) and the financier Angelo Ferrari.
facts.quote: However, delays followed due to financial difficulties, arguments regarding the location, the death of Tamburini in 1891, the murder of Meano in 1904 and the death of Angelo Ferrari, an Italian businessman who was financing the new theatre.

facts.fact: The Belgian architect Julio Dormal finished it in 1908, changing some of the structure and leaving his mark in the French style of the decoration.
facts.quote: The building was finally completed in 1908 under the direction of the Belgian architect Julio Dormal who made some changes in the structure and left his mark in the French style of the decoration.

facts.fact: The bas-reliefs and busts on the facade are by sculptor Luigi Trinchero.
facts.quote: The bas-reliefs and busts on the facade are the work of sculptor Luigi Trinchero.

facts.fact: It was declared a National Historic Monument in 1989.
facts.quote: The theatre was declared a National Historic Monument in 1989.

facts.fact: The theatre was closed for refurbishment from October 2006 to May 2010.
facts.quote: After an initial start of works to restore the landmark in 2005, the theatre was closed for refurbishment from October 2006 to May 2010.

facts.fact: Oscar Niemeyer designed the cathedral and structural engineer Joaquim Cardozo engineered it; it was completed and dedicated on 31 May 1970.
facts.quote: It was designed by Brazilian architect Oscar Niemeyer and engineered by Brazilian structural engineer Joaquim Cardozo, and was completed and dedicated on May 31, 1970.

facts.fact: The cathedral is a hyperboloid structure built from 16 concrete columns weighing 90 tons each.
facts.quote: The cathedral is a hyperboloid structure constructed from 16 concrete columns weighing 90 tons each.

facts.fact: Visitors enter through a tunnel and emerge into a bright space with a glass roof.
facts.quote: Visitors enter into the cathedral through a tunnel and emerge into a bright space with a glass roof.

facts.fact: The roof is made of 16 fibreglass pieces inserted between the concrete pillars, with a large stained glass work suspended beneath.
facts.quote: The outer roof of the cathedral is composed of 16 pieces of fiberglass, each 10 meters (33 ft) wide at the base and 30 meters (98 ft) long inserted between the concrete pillars. Under this is suspended a 2,000-square-meter (22,000 sq ft) stained glass work created in 1990 by Marianne Peretti in shades of blue, green, white and brown.

facts.fact: A reflecting pool around the roof helps cool the building, and visitors pass under it when entering.
facts.quote: A 12-meter (39 ft) wide, 40-centimeter (16 in) deep reflecting pool surrounds the cathedral roof and helps cool the building. Visitors pass under this pool when entering the cathedral.

facts.fact: Three angel sculptures hang over the nave from steel cables.
facts.quote: Over the nave are sculptures of three angels suspended by steel cables.

facts.fact: The cathedral can hold up to 4,000 people.
facts.quote: The cathedral can hold up to 4,000 people.

facts.fact: Four bronze Evangelist sculptures stand in the access square.
facts.quote: In the square access to the cathedral are four 2.5-meter (8 ft 2 in) tall bronze sculptures representing the four Evangelists, created by sculptors Alfredo Ceschiatti and Dante Croce in 1968.

facts.fact: Irish architect and furniture designer Eileen Gray and architect Jean Badovici designed and built E-1027 between 1926 and 1929.
facts.quote: It was designed and built from 1926–1929 by the Irish architect and furniture designer Eileen Gray and the French/Romanian Architect Jean Badovici.

facts.fact: It is L-shaped and flat-roofed, with floor-to-ceiling windows and a spiral stairway to the guest room, both open and compact.
facts.quote: L-shaped and flat-roofed with floor-to-ceiling windows and a spiral stairway to the guest room, E-1027 was both open and compact.

facts.fact: It is considered Gray's first major work, blurring the border between architecture and decoration and tailored to the lifestyle of its intended occupants.
facts.quote: This is considered to be Gray's first major work, making indistinct the border between architecture and decoration, and highly personalized to be in accord with the lifestyle of its intended occupants.

facts.fact: The name is a code: E for Eileen, 10 for Jean, 2 for Badovici and 7 for Gray.
facts.quote: The name of the house, E-1027, is a code of Eileen Gray and Jean Badovici ('E' standing for Eileen, '10' Jean, '2' Badovici, '7' Gray), reflecting their relationship as lovers during its construction.

facts.fact: It is impossible to identify the exact individual contributions of Gray and Badovici.
facts.quote: It is impossible to identify the exact individual contributions of Gray or Badovici to E-1027.

facts.fact: Gray also designed furniture for the house, including a tubular steel table with an adjustable top that caught crumbs.
facts.quote: Gray also designed furniture for the house, including a tubular steel table which would enable her sister to eat breakfast in bed without leaving crumbs on sheets, due to an adjustable top that caught the crumbs.

facts.fact: Le Corbusier painted murals on the white walls in 1938 and 1939, which Gray considered vandalism.
facts.quote: While staying as a guest of Badovici in his house in 1938 and 1939, Le Corbusier painted bright murals on its plain white walls with his permission, sometimes in the nude. That change to her ex-lover's house infuriated Gray, who considered the murals outright vandalism.

facts.fact: After a lengthy restoration it opened to the public in July 2021.
facts.quote: After its lengthy restoration, E-1027 opened to the public in July 2021.

facts.fact: The Queen Elizabeth Hall opened in 1967 on the South Bank in London with a concert conducted by Benjamin Britten.
facts.quote: The Queen Elizabeth Hall (QEH) is a music venue on the South Bank in London, England, that hosts classical, jazz, and avant-garde music, talks and dance performances. It was opened in 1967, with a concert conducted by Benjamin Britten.

facts.fact: The QEH and the smaller Purcell Room were built together as part of the Southbank Centre, beside the Royal Festival Hall and the Hayward Gallery.
facts.quote: The QEH was built along with the smaller Purcell Room as part of Southbank Centre arts complex.

facts.fact: A team led by Hubert Bennett of the Greater London Council's architects department, with Jack Whittle, F. G. West and Geoffrey Horsefall, designed the two auditoriums.
facts.quote: The two auditoriums were designed by a team led by Hubert Bennett, head of the architects department of the Greater London Council, with Jack Whittle, F.G. West and Geoffrey Horsefall.

facts.fact: The design shows the separate masses and elements of the building so as not to compete with the scale of the Royal Festival Hall.
facts.quote: The design of the QEH was intended to show to a high degree the separate masses and elements of the building, to avoid competing with the scale and presence of the RFH.

facts.fact: It uses minimal decoration and was designed for circulation at multiple levels around the building.
facts.quote: The QEH uses minimal decoration and was designed to allow circulation at multiple levels around the building.

facts.fact: The powerful forms and austere materials are an example of brutalist architecture, highlighting the plasticity of concrete.
facts.quote: The original arrangements provided for circulation above and below the foyer (no longer allowed for security reasons, although the roof terrace has been opened for the Summer of Fun festival in 2011), right around the sides and rear of the two auditoriums, and also a bridge link to the Hayward Gallery. The powerful forms and austere materials are an example of brutalist architecture, and the design also highlights the plasticity of concrete.

facts.fact: The foyer is a vee-shaped building raised on octagonal concrete columns, linked to the auditorium by cast concrete tubes reminiscent of a spaceship's docking arrangement.
facts.quote: The foyer is at first-floor level, and the foyer building is supported on octagonal reinforced concrete columns, with an undercroft below, and is vee-shaped. The two arms of the vee-shape are linked to the QEH auditorium by cast concrete tubes, reminiscent of a spaceship's docking arrangement.

facts.fact: The auditorium is a separate building, with the seating cantilevered out towards the foyer on a massive column holding the emergency stairs.
facts.quote: The QEH auditorium is a separate building from the foyer. The auditorium building is aligned with the rear of its stage parallel to Waterloo Bridge and the seating area cantilevered out towards the foyer, supported by a massive column containing the emergency escape staircases at the rear.

facts.fact: The undercroft has been popular with skateboarders since the early 1970s, a 'found space' widely acknowledged as London's most distinctive skateboarding area.
facts.quote: The undercroft of the foyer building has been popular with skateboarders since the early 1970s and it is widely acknowledged to be London's most distinctive and popular skateboarding area.

facts.fact: John Lautner designed the Chemosphere, a modernist house in Los Angeles, in 1960.
facts.quote: The Chemosphere is a modernist house at 7776 Torreyson Drive in Los Angeles, California, designed by John Lautner in 1960.

facts.fact: It is admired for the ingenuity of its solution to the site and for its unique octagonal design.
facts.quote: The building, which the Encyclopædia Britannica once called "the most modern home built in the world", is admired both for the ingenuity of its solution to the problem of the site and for its unique octagonal design.

facts.fact: It is a one-storey octagon with around 2,200 square feet of living space.
facts.quote: It is a one-story octagon with around 2,200 square feet (200 m2) of living space.

facts.fact: The octagon on a column was Lautner's solution to a site with a slope of 45 degrees that was thought practically unbuildable.
facts.quote: Most distinctively, the house is perched atop a 5-foot-wide (1.5 m) concrete column nearly 30 feet (9 m) high. This design was Lautner's solution to a site that, with a slope of 45 degrees, was thought to be practically unbuildable.

facts.fact: A concrete pedestal buried under the earth supports the column, and the house has survived earthquakes and heavy rains; it is reached by a funicular.
facts.quote: Because of a concrete pedestal, almost 20 feet (6 m) in diameter, buried under the earth and supporting the column, the house has survived earthquakes and heavy rains. The house is reached by a funicular.

facts.fact: The house is bisected by a central exposed brick wall with a fireplace.
facts.quote: Chemosphere is bisected by a central exposed brick wall with a fireplace, abutted by subdued seating, in the middle.

facts.fact: The lot was given to a young aerospace engineer, Leonard Malin, by his father-in-law, and he was determined to live there despite limited means.
facts.quote: The lot had been given to a young aerospace engineer by his father-in-law; despite his own limited means, the engineer, Leonard Malin, was determined to live there.

facts.fact: The cost was subsidised partly by barter with two sponsoring companies; Chem Seal supplied experimental coatings and resins and inspired the name, though Lautner originally wanted to call it Chapiteau.
facts.quote: The cost to build Chemosphere, $140,000 (equivalent to $1.52 million in 2025), was subsidized partly by barter with two sponsoring companies, the Southern California Gas Company and the Chem Seal Corporation. Chem Seal provided the experimental coatings and resins to put the house together and inspired the name Chemosphere. (Lautner originally wanted to call the house Chapiteau.

facts.fact: The Custom House is a neoclassical 18th-century building on the north bank of the River Liffey in Dublin, now housing a government department.
facts.quote: The Custom House (Irish: Teach an Chustaim) is a neoclassical 18th century building in Dublin, Ireland which houses the Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage.

facts.fact: The new Custom House was the idea of John Beresford, who became first commissioner of revenue for Ireland in 1780.
facts.quote: The building of a new Custom House for Dublin was the idea of John Beresford, who became the first commissioner of revenue for Ireland in 1780.

facts.fact: James Gandon was appointed architect in 1781 after the original architect, Thomas Cooley, died; it was Gandon's first large-scale commission.
facts.quote: In 1781 he appointed James Gandon as architect, after Thomas Cooley, the original architect on the project, had died. This was Gandon's first large-scale commission.

facts.fact: Dublin Corporation and some merchants opposed it, complaining that it moved the axis of the city, left little room for shipping and was built on a swamp.
facts.quote: The new Custom House was unpopular with the Dublin Corporation and some city merchants who complained that it moved the axis of the city, would leave little room for shipping, and was being built on what at the time was a swamp and is detailed as reclaimed land on John Roque's 1756 map of Dublin as being part of Amory's Grant.

facts.fact: Foundation work was disrupted by a mob led by the High Sheriff and members of the Dublin Corporation, but Beresford ignored the protests.
facts.quote: Purchase of land was delayed and proved exorbitant and the laying of foundations was disrupted by the High Sheriff and members of the Dublin Corporation with a mob of several thousand. However, Beresford was determined to complete the project and ignored the protests.

facts.fact: Gandon used Irish artists and craftsmen as assistants, and every available mason in Dublin was engaged.
facts.quote: Construction started in 1781, and for his assistants, Gandon chose Irish artists such as Meath stone-cutter Henry Darley, mason John Semple and carpenter Hugh Henry. Every available mason in Dublin was engaged in the work.

facts.fact: The four facades are decorated with coats-of-arms and ornamental sculptures by Edward Smyth representing Ireland's rivers.
facts.quote: The four facades of the building are decorated with coats-of-arms and ornamental sculptures (by Edward Smyth) representing Ireland's rivers.

facts.fact: Achyut Kanvinde was the architect of the ATIRA building.
facts.quote: The architect of the ATIRA building is Achyut Kanvinde.

facts.fact: The foundation stone was laid in 1950 and the complex was inaugurated by Jawaharlal Nehru in 1954.
facts.quote: The foundation stone for the ATIRA complex was laid by Vallabhbhai Patel on 1 November 1950 which was inaugurated by the then Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru on completion on 10 April 1954.

facts.fact: The building's exterior is described as influenced by Walter Gropius.
facts.quote: The exterior of the building are influenced by Walter Gropius.

facts.fact: ATIRA was conceived by Vikram Sarabhai, Kasturbhai Lalbhai and Shanti Swaroop Bhatnagar.
facts.quote: The idea of ATIRA was conceived by Vikram Sarabhai, Kasturbhai Lalbhai and Shanti Swaroop Bhatnagar.

facts.fact: The Hedmark museum in Hamar is a regional museum that includes the medieval cathedral ruins mentioned in Sigrid Undset's Kristin Lavransdatter.
facts.quote: Anno Museum (formerly Hedmarks fylkesmuseum) in Hamar, Norway, is a regional museum for the municipalities of Stange, Hamar, Løten, and Ringsaker in central eastern Norway. It includes the medieval Cathedral Ruins in Hamar mentioned in Sigrid Undset's literary magnum opus Kristin Lavransdatter.

facts.fact: Storhamarlåven was designed by Sverre Fehn in concrete, wood and glass to contrast with the stone of the medieval ruins.
facts.quote: Storhamarlåven was designed by architect Sverre Fehn (1924–2009) in concrete, wood and glass to contrast with the stone of the medieval ruins.

facts.fact: It was originally a barn built beside the ruins in the 17th century for the farm Storhamar.
facts.quote: It was originally a barn built beside the ruins in the 17th century for the farm Storhamar.

facts.fact: The architect sought to highlight both the original medieval structure and the more recent farm building.
facts.quote: The architect sought to both highlight the original medieval structure and the more recent farm building.

facts.fact: Ramps provide the means to view the museum from above.
facts.quote: Ramps provide the means to view the museum from above.

facts.fact: Its design won the Betongtavlen architectural award in 1976.
facts.quote: Its design won the Betongtavlen architectural award in 1976.

facts.fact: The cathedral ruins are secured under a glass shelter designed by Lund & Slaatto and completed in 1998.
facts.quote: The cathedral ruins are secured under a glass shelter designed by Lund & Slaatto Architects and completed in 1998.
